competencies.title: Calibrating professional judgment in human-AI collaboration
competencies.description: Developing and maintaining accurate self-assessment of when to trust, qualify, or override AI outputs — avoiding both automation bias (over-trust) and automation skepticism (under-trust) — through deliberate reflection on the outcomes of past judgment calls.

tasks.text: Assess the reliability profile of an AI tool by systematically comparing its outputs to independent evidence across a range of conditions, building a calibrated mental model of where and how the tool fails

Apply calibrated trust in operational contexts — accepting AI outputs when within the validated reliability envelope, qualifying them when near its edges, and overriding them when outside it — while documenting the basis of each judgment call
Evaluate past trust decisions against observed outcomes to update calibration, identify systematic biases in one's own judgment under automation pressure, and revise decision heuristics accordingly

proficiency.knowledge: Understands automation bias as a professional risk — the tendency to defer to AI outputs even when independent judgment should override; understands automation skepticism as the symmetric failure; recognizes that calibration requires active effort and deteriorates without deliberate maintenance
proficiency.application: Identifies situations where they may be at risk of automation bias; applies explicit decision checkpoints before accepting AI outputs in high-consequence contexts

indicators.text: Explains automation bias and automation skepticism as distinct failure modes with different consequences in environmental management contexts
Identifies the categories of AI output in their work context that carry the highest consequence if accepted without adequate validation
Applies a structured decision checkpoint before accepting AI outputs in high-consequence contexts — naming the independent evidence they are drawing on
Recognizes when time pressure, organizational culture, or workflow design is creating conditions for automation bias to operate

proficiency.knowledge: Applies systematic reliability assessment to build calibrated mental models of specific AI tools; understands how training data distribution, model architecture, and deployment context determine where AI tools are reliable and where they fail; recognizes institutional conditions that erode calibration
proficiency.application: Conducts reliability assessments for AI tools in their operational context; maintains documented calibration records; applies calibrated trust consistently across the range of operating conditions encountered

indicators.text: Conducts systematic reliability assessment for an AI tool — testing outputs across varying conditions to map the reliability envelope
Builds a calibrated mental model of a specific AI tool's failure modes and communicates it to colleagues and supervisors
Maintains calibration under institutional pressure to accept AI outputs more readily than reliability warrants
Documents trust decisions and their basis in a format that supports retrospective calibration review

proficiency.knowledge: Expert in calibration methodology and its application across multiple AI tool types; deep understanding of the organizational and workflow conditions that produce and erode calibration; experienced in advising teams on calibration practices and identifying systematic bias patterns
proficiency.application: Designs organizational calibration programs; identifies and corrects systematic calibration failures at team level; advises on workflow and tool deployment conditions that protect calibration quality

indicators.text: Designs team-level calibration programs — defining reliability assessment protocols, calibration review schedules, and documentation standards for AI tools in operational use
Identifies systematic calibration failures — patterns indicating that a team is operating outside an AI tool's validated reliability envelope without recognizing it
Advises on workflow conditions that protect calibration quality, including workload, time pressure, and escalation pathway design
Conducts retrospective calibration reviews using outcome data to identify systematic biases in past judgment and redesign decision heuristics

proficiency.knowledge: Shapes field-wide frameworks for calibration practice in AI-augmented environmental management; recognized authority on automation bias, calibration methodology, and the institutional conditions that enable and undermine calibrated human-AI collaboration
proficiency.application: Advances professional standards for calibration practice; contributes to regulatory guidance on human oversight requirements in AI-assisted environmental decision-making

indicators.text: Contributes to development of professional or regulatory standards for human oversight requirements and calibration obligations in AI-assisted environmental applications
Publishes or presents on automation bias patterns, calibration methodology, and institutional conditions affecting human-AI judgment quality in environmental management
Advises agencies and organizations on calibration program design and the workflow conditions required to maintain calibrated human oversight of AI systems
Recognized as a leading practitioner in human-AI calibration practice in environmental management contexts

data_dictionary.field: The Dimension Tags sheet contains five ethical lens columns (L1–L5) that classify each competency's relationship to five ethical dimensions of environmental management practice. These columns are currently empty. Classification of all 222 competencies is complete in session working records (Tasks 15 and 14); database population is in progress.

data_dictionary.sheet: The obligation to examine who bears the costs and receives the benefits of environmental decisions, including distributive, procedural, and recognition justice dimensions.

Indigenous peoples' collective rights to govern decisions affecting their lands, knowledge, and data — including FPIC, data sovereignty (CARE Principles), and self-determined participation. Distinct from L1: a project can distribute benefits equitably while still violating governance rights.
The obligation to make decisions, analyses, and their basis visible, and to ensure that someone bears consequence for decisions affecting others.

The ethics of deliberate ecological manipulation — whether intervention is justified, at what scale, with whose authorization, and with what obligations regarding reversibility and precaution. Triggers when management action creates conditions without historical precedent or is practically irreversible.

Obligations practitioners carry when institutional pressures conflict with duties to the public and to ecological systems — including honest reporting, conflict-of-interest disclosure, and the conditions under which professional deference to organizational authority is or is not appropriate.
The ethical dimension is named, operationalized, or directly engaged in the competency's proficiency indicators or job tasks.

The ethical dimension is structurally present but unnamed — a practitioner exercising the competency confronts the ethical issue without the competency providing vocabulary or decision criteria for it.
The ethical dimension is not meaningfully engaged by the competency.
Not yet populated (pending database integration from session records).

data_dictionary.field: Skill Area 7.1 (Professional Ethics Architecture) uses E/A only — no Implicit values. These competencies were designed to make ethical content constitutive, so the E/A binary applies a constitutive test: E means removing the lens would collapse the competency's argument. Skill Area 7.2 (Human-AI Professional Practice) uses the standard E/I/A vocabulary.

Across the taxonomy, approximately 95% of ethical content is implicit rather than explicit. This ratio is itself a significant finding — it indicates that existing professional competency standards embed ethical obligations in practice without providing practitioners shared vocabulary for recognizing or reasoning about them. Intervention Ethics (L4) has zero explicit treatments in Domains 1–6 despite governing high-consequence ecological decisions.

Domain-specific ethical lens classification records from Tasks 15 (Domains 1–6) and 14 (Domain 7). Task 15 working documents used transposed L2/L3 numbering; the Lens Numbering Correction Note (above) applies when transcribing from those records.
